question: Assuming Gareth Evan's Generality Constraint, if I understand a proposition Fa, should I be able to understand Fx (\forall x)? Assume I understand universal quantification.

1.text:
No. The generality constraint does not give you ∀x Fx.

On Evans's view the constraint is about repeatability / generality of thought, not about universal closure. If you think that a is F you must be able to think of F as a repeatable, general property that can be entertained with a variable. That is, thinking Fa is possible only if you can think the schema Fx for a free variable x, and can in principle substitute for x, and can think of a as falling under F in the same general way that other things could fall under F.

That is compatible with being unable to evaluate or fully understand the universal generalisation ∀x Fx. Understanding ∀x Fx as a truth-evaluable claim about the domain requires knowing the range of the quantifier and that F holds of every object in that range, or being able to entertain the general thought under the quantifier. Knowing that F holds of one particular object a gives you no purchase on whether it holds of b, c, ... The schema Fx is now open, but ∀x Fx is a further, substantive claim about the extension of F.

Even on the charitable assumption that the formal operation of universal quantification is understood in the purely syntactic sense, to understand the content of ∀x Fx you would need a grasp of the domain and of F as holding throughout it. Evans's constraint only requires that F be operative in a general manner so that the thought that a is F can be thought as an instance of the general thought that something is F, not that you can think that everything is F.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: No, not ∀x Fx.

The Generality Constraint is a constraint on the *form* in which a thought can be entertained, not a licence to infer a substantial universal from a singular instance.

If you can entertain the singular thought that a is F you must be able to entertain that thought in a way which is generality-entertaining with respect to the constituent a. That is, you must be able to think of a under a mode of presentation that is capable of being caught by a variable, and so you can entertain the thought under the schema `F x` with x playing the role of the thing you are thinking about, and in particular you can entertain the trivial generalisation 
∀x(x = a → Fx)
or, essentially, the thought that the object you are thinking of satisfies F.

It does not give you the substantive generalisation ∀x Fx, i.e. that F holds of every object. Generality-entertainability for a guarantees you can replace the particular singular term a by a variable which can be made to range over the object a, not that you can range over all objects and assert F of them. Even granted that you know what the universal quantifier means, you still need independent warrant that F is true of all x in order to be able to entertain ∀x Fx as a true thought. The constraint only requires a way of thinking about a which is of the form `λx[Fx & ...]` so that you can think of an object indistinguishably of a under the same concept; it does not turn the singular instance Fa into the universal claim that everything is F.

Hence you can entertain the variable form of the thought about a, but you do not thereby have to be able to entertain the distinct proposition ∀x Fx.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: No, not the universal closure.

Evans' Generality Constraint is a constraint on the form of thinkable contents, not on what you are entitled to infer. It says that if a thinker can entertain the singular thought that a is F then the thinker must be in a position to entertain the thought under a variable. In particular the concept F which figures in the singular thought must be available to the thinker as a general, systematic concept that can be combined with a variable, i.e. the thinker must be able to entertain the schema Fx, and in the usual formulation the closed form ∃x[Fx ∧ x=a] which makes explicit that a is the value of the variable under which F is thought.

That is a requirement of systematicity of thought rather than a requirement of truth. The ability to think Fa already presupposes a grasp of F as a property that can be predicated of an arbitrary object, hence the thinker can entertain Fx with x free, and can entertain thoughts formed by binding that variable with the usual operators.

It does not require that the thinker be able to entertain, let alone assent to, the universal generalisation ∀x Fx. From Fa nothing follows about other objects, and the generality constraint imposes no epistemic commitment to the extension of F. Even granting that the subject understands the universal quantifier as a formal device, understanding ∀x Fx is understanding the claim that every object in the domain is F. That claim is not a condition of being able to think Fa, and the capacity to think the schema Fx is compatible with not knowing, and indeed with knowing that, ∀x Fx is false. The constraint is about being able to think of a with a variable, not about being able to universalise over the domain of F.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Yes, on Evans’ reading that is just what the Generality Constraint is.

For Evans to understand ‘Fa’ is to possess the concept F and to be able to apply it to the particular object a in the thought that a is F. Possessing a concept is not possessing it only in an a-tethered way. If a thinker can entertain the singular thought Fa he must have the concept F in a form that is deployable independently of the particular singular mode of presentation of a. That is the Generality Constraint: the content of a thought with a singular term must be such that the thinker can think the same matter of F with the term replaced by a variable.

Hence competence with Fa commits you to the general concept Fx, i.e. to being able to entertain the open formula ‘x is F’ and to substitute any individual into it, in particular to be able to think Fb for any b for which the thought makes sense. That is the core of generality.

If you in addition understand the universal quantifier as an operator on open sentences, you can combine the general concept you already have with ∀ to entertain the closed thought ∀x Fx. To understand ∀x Fx in Evans’ sense is just to be able to entertain the general thought that F is held fixed while the variable ranges over objects, not to believe or know that it is true, nor to be able to evaluate it in the actual domain. The Generality Constraint gives you the Fx part; understanding of quantification gives you the ∀ part.

No. The Generality Constraint is about the form of the mode of presentation you are using, not about the truth content you are committed to.

For Evans a singular thought that a is F is possible for a subject S only if F can be deployed by S in a position that is independent of the particular singular mode ‘a’, i.e. under a genuinely general mode of presentation. That is S must be able to think the open schema Fx with a free variable and to operate with the concept F in the position of an argument place so that a can be substituted for x and x can be substituted for a in other thoughts.

In particular S must be able to think

x = a -> Fx

and indeed to think Fx as a schema and to think there is an x such that x = a & Fx. It does not require S to be able to think, still less to think truly, the universal closure ∀x Fx. Understanding Fa gives you understanding of the concept F and of the singular mode a. Assumed understanding of the universal quantifier gives you the ability in principle to combine the concept F with ∀. That is a formal ability to form the sentence ∀x Fx, but the Generality Constraint does not make the content ∀x Fx a condition for understanding Fa. The generalizability required by Evans is generalizability of the mode of presentation of F and of the argument place, not generalizability of the truth value of the predication to the whole domain. The universal claim ∀x Fx is a distinct thought with a distinct content from the singular instance Fa and can be false even if Fa is true.

6.text:
Under the Generality Constraint a thought with an object-constituent commits you to possessing the other constituents as general concepts. 

If you really think that a is F you must possess the concept F independently of the particular thought about a. Possessing F is more than being able to apply it once to a: it is being able to apply it, in principle, to any object you can think about. That is the ability to entertain the schema

x is F

and to vary the object place while keeping the property place fixed. In Evans’ terms you cannot have the particular thought Fa without being able to think thoughts of the form Fx and, in particular, the thought that something is F.

That is already the generality requirement. Given that you already possess the logical concept of universal quantification, the closed sentence

∀x Fx

is a syntactic combination of a concept you now have to possess, F, with a quantificational operator you are assumed to understand. The constraint therefore commits you to being able to understand the general form Fx, and with quantifier competence to being able to understand the closed form ∀x Fx as a thought you can entertain. 

The constraint secures possession of the concept F only, not the truth of the universal. You may be able to understand ∀x Fx while being ignorant of its truth-value or of the domain over which x ranges. What is required is conceptual generality, not epistemic omniscience about the extension of F.

Under a standard reading of Evans the Generality Constraint is a constraint on
the mode of presentation under which a thinker can think of an object, not a
constraint on what the thinker is committed to be true about the property.

If S can think the singular thought that a is F then S must be able to think
of a under the concept F in a way that is not essentially tied to the
singular term ‘a’. In Evans’ terms S must be able to think the thought in the
general form

     x is F

with ‘x’ a free variable that can be instantiated by a and by other objects,
and hence to think of F as a general property that can be predicated of an
arbitrary thing. That is the ability to re-describe the content of Fa as
F(a) and to move to the schema Fx.

That does not by itself commit S to the truth of the universal
generalisation

     ∀x Fx

or even to the existential generalisation ∃x Fx. The ability to put the
concept F under a variable is the ability to think of F in abstraction from
the particular object a, i.e. to be able to entertain ‘something is F’, ‘x is
F for x = a’, ‘x is F for x = b’, etc., and in particular to think the
conditional

     ∀x [x = a → Fx]

that is just Fa in general form. 

On the supposition that S does in fact understand the quantifier ∀ the
mechanistic formation ∀x Fx is syntactically available to S, but Evans does
not require S to have, nor to accept, the content that everything is F in
order to understand that a is F. Understanding Fa requires generalisability of
F, i.e. the ability to entertain Fx for an arbitrary x, not the endorsement
of the universal proposition ∀x Fx. The requirement is the former: F has to
be thinkable as a general concept, not that the thinker must think that F is
instantiated by every object.

The question is whether Evans’ Generality Constraint, together with assumed competence with ∀, makes understanding Fa sufficient for being able to understand the proposition ∀x Fx.

Round 0 positions are split.

No/negative camp: Colleagues 1,2,3,5,8. Core claim: Generality Constraint is a constraint on the form/mode of presentation of a thought, not on its truth content or on epistemic warrant. If you can think Fa you must be able to think of F as a repeatable/general concept and to entertain the open schema Fx for a free variable x, in effect thoughts such as ∀x(x=a→Fx), ∃x[Fx∧x=a], or the ability to substitute for x while keeping F fixed. That secures systematicity and the ability to think of a under a general mode of presentation. It does not give you substantive generalisation about other objects. Understanding ∀x Fx requires grasp of the domain and a commitment that F holds of every object in the range. Fa gives no purchase on b,c,… Even with pure syntactic understanding of ∀, understanding the content of ∀x Fx is distinct from and stronger than grasping Fx as a schema. Hence the constraint is compatible with not knowing, and even knowing, ∀x Fx is false.

Yes/affirmative camp: Colleagues 4,6,7. Core claim: Possessing concept F on Evans’ view is possessing it generally, i.e. as deployable with a variable. If you understand Fa you must already possess F as a general concept Fx. If you also understand the universal quantifier as an operator on open sentences, you can in principle close the schema to ∀x Fx. * Schema Fx / general entertainability vs closed universal proposition ∀x Fx.
* Ability to form/entertain a thought vs truth belief/knowledge of truth value / epistemic commitment.
* Generalizability of the mode of presentation of F and of the argument place vs generalizability of the truth of the predication to the whole domain.
